- [passage] | Field | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | `distinct` | string | The name of the collection to query for distinct values. | | `key` | string | The field for which to return distinct values. | | `query` | document | Optional. A query that specifies the documents from which to retrieve the distinct values. | | `readConcern` | document | Optional. Specifies the [read concern.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/glossary.md#std-term-read-concern) The `readConcern` option has the following syntax: `readConcern: { level: <value> }` Possible read concern levels are: [`"local"`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/read-concern-local.md#mongodb-readconcern-readconcern.-local-). This is the default read concern level for read operations against the primary and secondaries.; [`"available"`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/read-concern-available.md#mongodb-readconcern-readconcern.-available-). Available for read operations against the primary and secondaries. [`"available"`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/read-concern-available.md#mongodb-readconcern-readconcern.-available-) behaves the same as [`"local"`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/read-concern-local.md#mongodb-readconcern-readconcern.-local-) against the primary and non-sharded secondaries. The query returns the instance's most recent data.; [`"majority"`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/read-concern-majority.md#mongodb-readconcern-readconcern.-majority-). Available for replica sets that use [WiredTiger storage engine.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/wiredtiger.md#std-label-storage-wiredtiger); [`"linearizable"`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/read-concern-linearizable.md#mongodb-readconcern-readconcern.-linearizable-). Available for read operations on the [`primary`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/replica-states.md#mongodb-replstate-replstate.PRIMARY) only.; [`"snapshot"`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/read-concern-snapshot.md#mongodb-readconcern-readconcern.-snapshot-). Available for [multi-document transactions](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/transactions.md#std-label-transactions) and certain read operations outside of multi-document transactions. For more formation on the read concern levels, see [Read Concern Levels.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/read-concern.md#std-label-read-concern-levels) | | `collation` | document | Optional. Optional. Specifies the [collation](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/collation.md#std-label-collation) to use for the operation. [Collation](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/collation.md#std-label-collation) allows users to specify language-specific rules for string comparison, such as rules for lettercase and accent marks. The collation option has the following syntax: `collation: { locale: <string>, caseLevel: <boolean>, caseFirst: <string>, strength: <int>, numericOrdering: <boolean>, alternate: <string>, maxVariable: <string>, backwards: <boolean> }` When specifying collation, the `locale` field is mandatory; all other collation fields are optional. For descriptions of the fields, see [Collation Document.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/collation.md#std-label-collation-document-fields) If the collation is unspecified but the collection has a default collation (see [`db.createCollection()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/db.createcollection.md#mongodb-method-db.createCollection)), the operation uses the collation specified for the collection. If no collation is specified for the collection or for the operations, MongoDB uses the simple binary comparison used in prior versions for string comparisons. You cannot specify multiple collations for an operation. For example, you cannot specify different collations per field, or if performing a find with a sort, you cannot use one collation for the find and another for the sort. | | `comment` | any | Optional. A user-provided comment to attach to this command. Once set, this comment appears alongside records of this command in the following locations: [mongod log messages](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/log-messages.md#std-label-log-messages-ref), in the `attr.command.cursor.comment` field.; [Database profiler](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/database-profiler.md#std-label-profiler) output, in the [`command.comment`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/database-profiler.md#mongodb-data-system.profile.command) field.; [`currentOp`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/currentop.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.currentOp) output, in the [`command.comment`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/currentop.md#mongodb-data-currentOp.command) field. A comment can be any valid [BSON type](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/bson-types.md#std-label-bson-types) (string, integer, object, array, etc). | | `hint` | string or document | Optional. Specify the index name, either as a string or a document. If specified, the query planner only considers plans using the hinted index. For more details, see [Specify an Index.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/distinct.md#std-label-index-example) **New in version 7.1** | | `querySettings` | document | Optional. Query settings that apply only to this execution of the command. The `querySettings` document accepts the following fields: `indexHints`; `queryFramework`; `reject`; `comment`; `queryKnobs`; `maxTimeMS` For descriptions of these fields, see [Command Fields.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/setquerysettings.md#std-label-setQuerySettings-fields) MongoDB doesn't store these settings on the cluster, and they don't apply to other queries with the same [query shape](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/query-shapes.md#std-label-query-shapes). To set query settings that persist for a query shape, use [`setQuerySettings`.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/setquerysettings.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.setQuerySettings) MongoDB combines the settings that you pass in the command with any query settings stored on the cluster for the same query shape. If both settings specify the same field, the stored cluster setting takes precedence. **New in version 9.0** | | `maxTimeMS` | non-negative integer | Optional. Specifies a time limit in milliseconds. If you do not specify a value for `maxTimeMS`, operations will not time out. A value of `0` explicitly specifies the default unbounded behavior. MongoDB terminates operations that exceed their allotted time limit using the same mechanism as [`db.killOp()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/db.killop.md#mongodb-method-db.killOp). MongoDB only terminates an operation at one of its designated [interrupt points.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/glossary.md#std-term-interrupt-point) | — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/distinct.md#command-fields · keywords: index, index selectivity, query planner, distinct, key, query
- [passage] If a document has a `null` or missing value for the indexed field in a unique single-field index, the index stores a `null` value for that document. Because of the unique constraint, a single-field unique index can only contain one document that contains a `null` value in its index entry. If there is more than one document with a `null` value in its index entry, the index build fails with a duplicate key error. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-unique.md#missing-document-field-in-a-unique-single-field-index · keywords: index, index key, single-field index, null
- [passage] However, the following query cannot use the index because it includes a null match on the `email` field, which is not permitted by the filter expression `{ email: { $exists: true } }`: — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-partial.md#comparison-with-sparse-indexes · keywords: index, sparse index, email, { email: { $exists: true } }
- [passage] Starting in MongoDB 9.0, if an indexed field becomes a multikey field while a query that references the field is running, the query might fail with a QueryKilledError. - [fact] In a compound multikey index, MongoDB compounds bounds across scalar-field keys and array-field keys. Example: {item: 1, ratings: 1} with item: 'XYZ', ratings: {$gte: 3} yields both bounds. If bounds cannot be compounded, MongoDB constrains the scan by the leading field only. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-multikey/multikey-index-bounds.md · keywords: index, multikey index, Multikey Indexes and Array Query Bounds
- [passage] For example, a comparison between `$a` and a constant value can use an index, but a comparison between `$a` and `$b` cannot. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/query/expr.md#expr-in-lookup-operations · keywords: $a, $b
- [passage] "Range" filters scan fields. The scan doesn't require an exact match, which means range filters are loosely bound to index keys. To improve query efficiency, limit the range bounds and use equality matches to reduce the number of documents to scan. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/equality-sort-range-rule/ · keywords: mongodb-compound-index-design

If your results exceed the maximum BSON size, use the aggregation pipeline to retrieve distinct values using the [`$group`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/group.md#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-group) operator, as described in [Retrieve Distinct Values with the Aggregation Pipeline.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/group.md#std-label-aggregation-group-distinct-values) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/db.collection.distinct.md#syntax · keywords: index selectivity, $group · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/distinct.md

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [fact] Placing sort fields before range fields lets the index return results in index order and avoids a blocking in-memory SORT stage. The trade-off is that more index keys may be scanned. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/equality-sort-range-rule/ · keywords: ESR rule, compound index, index, index key, sort direction, Compound Indexes and ESR Rule
- [statement] Alex Bevi's explain examples show the trade-off. With sort on region and range on joined, {joined:1, region:1} examined 4 keys and used an in-memory SORT stage. {region:1, joined:1} examined 5 keys with no blocking sort. He also says equality fields need not be ordered from most to least selective. — https://alexbevi.com/blog/2020/05/16/optimizing-mongodb-compound-indexes-the-equality-sort-range-esr-rule/ · keywords: ESR rule, compound index, index, query planner, sort direction, Compound Indexes and ESR Rule
- [fact] A single-field index whose key is the leading prefix of a compound index (e.g. {field:1} next to {field:1, other:1}) is redundant: the compound index serves the same filter. Keep the compound index and drop the prefix one. The manual's example drops {time:1} as covered by {day:1, time:1}, though that example's field names are inconsistent (days vs day). — https://mongodb.com/docs/manual/data-modeling/design-antipatterns/unnecessary-indexes/ · keywords: compound index, covered query, index, index anti-pattern, single-field index, Index Anti-Patterns

This option can enforce a smaller limit than 16 MiB, but not a larger one. When set, the `batchSize` is the lesser of `batchSize` documents or 16 MiB worth of documents. The document syntax is: `{ <variable_name_1>: <expression_1>, ..., <variable_name_n>: <expression_n> }` The variable is set to the value returned by the expression, and cannot be changed afterwards. To set query settings that persist for a query shape, use [`setQuerySettings`.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/setquerysettings.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.setQuerySettings) MongoDB combines the settings that you pass in the command with any query settings stored on the cluster for the same query shape. - [passage] Use partial indexes instead of [sparse indexes](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-sparse.md#std-label-index-type-sparse) for more precise control over which documents to index: — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-partial.md#comparison-with-sparse-indexes · keywords: index, partial index, sparse index
- [passage] The second compound index, `{ rated: 1, year: 1 }`, is therefore the more efficient index for supporting the example query, as the MongoDB server only needs to scan `235` [`index keys`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/explain-results.md#mongodb-data-explain.executionStats.totalKeysExamined) to find all matching documents using this index, compared to `246` when using the compound index `{ year: 1, rated: 1 }`. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/analyze-query-plan.md#mongodb-shell · keywords: compound index, index, index key, { rated: 1, year: 1 }, 235, index keys · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/analyze-query-plan/
- [passage] Sparse indexes in MongoDB differ from [block-level](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Database_index#Sparse_index) sparse indexes in other databases. Sparse indexes only contain entries for documents that have the indexed field, even if the index field contains a null value. The index skips over any document that is missing the indexed field. The index is "sparse" because it does not include all documents of a collection. By contrast, non-sparse indexes contain all documents in a collection, storing null values for those documents that do not contain the indexed field. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-sparse.md · keywords: index, index key, sparse index
- [fact] Since MongoDB 3.3.8 (SERVER-15086), the server tracks multikey status per path rather than one flag per index. This lets the planner apply both bounds on a scalar leading field of a compound multikey index. Before that, it could bound only one side and filtered the rest after FETCH. explain now shows multiKeyPaths on IXSCAN. The change covers WiredTiger and in-memory engines. — https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-15086 · keywords: index, multikey index, query planner, Multikey Indexes and Array Query Bounds
- [passage] | Field | Field Type | Necessity | Description | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `setQuerySettings` | document or string | Required | You can provide either: The same fields as those in a [`find`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/find.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.find), [`distinct`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/distinct.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.distinct), or [`aggregate`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/aggregate.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.aggregate) command, and a `$db` field with the database associated with the original command.; An existing query shape hash string that uniquely identifies the query shape. An example query shape hash is `"F42757F1AEB68B4C5A6DE6182B29B01947C829C926BCC01226BDA4DDE799766C"``. | | `indexHints.ns` | document | Optional | Namespace for index hints. Only required when optional index hints are specified. | | `indexHints.ns.db` | string | Conditional | Name of the database for the index hints. Required when you specify `indexHints.ns`. | | `indexHints.ns.coll` | string | Conditional | Name of the collection for the index hints. Required when you specify `indexHints.ns`. | | `indexHints.allowedIndexes` | array | Optional | Array of indexes for index hints. An index hint can be one of these: Index name; index key pattern; [`$natural`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.hint.md#mongodb-operator-metaOp.-natural) hint For more details, see [Indexes](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/indexes.md#std-label-indexes) and [`hint()`.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.hint.md#mongodb-method-cursor.hint) | | `queryFramework` | string | Optional | [Query framework](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/glossary.md#std-term-query-framework) string can be set to: `classic` to use the classic engine.; `sbe` to use slot-based query execution engine. For details, see [Slot-Based Query Execution Engine.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/sbe.md#std-label-sbe-landing) | | `reject` | boolean | Optional | If `true`: New queries with the matching query shape are rejected and the query response states the query is rejected.; Any queries currently in progress aren't rejected. Default is `false`. To enable a query shape, run `setQuerySettings` again for the query shape and set `reject` to `false`. If you set `reject` to `true` and then back to `false` using `setQuerySettings` then: If your `settings` document isn't empty, then `setQuerySettings` enables the query shape.; If your `settings` document only contains `reject: false`, then `setQuerySettings` returns an error. Instead, use the `removeQuerySettings` command to remove the settings and then use `setQuerySettings` to add query settings. | | `comment` | BSON type | Optional | A comment can be any valid [BSON type](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/bson-types.md#std-label-bson-types). For example: string, object, and so on. You can use a comment to provide additional information about the query settings. For example, to add a string that indicates why you added the query settings, use `comment: "Index hint for orderDate_1 index to improve query performance"`. To update a comment, run `setQuerySettings` again and use `comment: { body: { msg: "Updated comment" } }`. You cannot remove a comment, but you can set it to a string with a space character. You can remove the query settings using [`removeQuerySettings`.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/removequerysettings.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.removeQuerySettings) Comments appear in the [`$querySettings`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/querysettings.md#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-querySettings) aggregation pipeline stage output, the [explain() command output](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/explain-results.md#std-label-explain-results), and the [slow query logs.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/log-messages.md#std-label-log-message-slow-ops) **New in version 8.1** (and 8.0.4). | | `queryKnobs` | document | Optional | A document of `{ <knobName>: <value> }` pairs that override internal server parameters for this query shape only, instead of instance-wide with [`setParameter`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/setparameter.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.setParameter). Each knob keeps the type, bounds, and default of its underlying server parameter. Unlike the other `setQuerySettings` fields, which replace the entire value when set, `queryKnobs` merges with existing knob values. `setQuerySettings` changes the knobs you include in the `queryKnobs` document, and leaves all other knobs unchanged. `queryKnobs: {}` results in a no-op. To remove a single knob without affecting the others, set that knob's value to `null`. **New in version 9.0** | | `maxTimeMS` | non-negative integer | Optional | Sets a time limit in milliseconds for executions of the [query shape](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/query-shapes.md#std-label-query-shapes). Use this setting to cap a single regressed shape or lift an over-tight client timeout without changing application code. If you omit `maxTimeMS` from query settings, the operation's timeout follows the command-level `maxTimeMS` option and the [`defaultMaxTimeMS`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/cluster-parameters/defaultmaxtimems.md#mongodb-parameter-param.defaultMaxTimeMS) cluster parameter. Setting `maxTimeMS` to `0` clears the `maxTimeMS` query setting, and the operation falls back to the command-level and cluster default values. A `maxTimeMS` value set with `setQuerySettings` takes precedence over a `maxTimeMS` value supplied in the command. **New in version 9.0** | — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/setQuerySettings.md#command-fields · keywords: index, index key, query planner, setQuerySettings, find, distinct
- [passage] To support this query, create one index on `runtime` and another index on `year`, rather than a compound index: — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/query/or.md#or-clauses-and-indexes · keywords: compound index, index, runtime, year · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/query/or/
- [passage] Compared to normal collections, storing time series data in time series collections improves query efficiency and reduces the disk usage for time series data and [secondary indexes](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/glossary.md#std-term-secondary-index). MongoDB 6.3 and later automatically creates a [compound index](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-compound.md#std-label-index-type-compound) on the time and metadata fields for new time series collections. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries-collections.md#benefits · keywords: compound index, index · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/timeseries-collections/
- [passage] | Option | Description | | --- | --- | | allowDiskUse | Whether or not pipelines that require more than 100 megabytes of memory to execute write to temporary files on disk. For details, see [`cursor.allowDiskUse()`.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.allowdiskuse.md#mongodb-method-cursor.allowDiskUse) | | allowPartialResults | For queries against a sharded collection, allows the command (or subsequent getMore commands) to return partial results, rather than an error, if one or more queried shards are unavailable. | | awaitData | If the cursor is a a tailable-await cursor. Requires `tailable` to be `true`. | | collation | Collation settings for update operation. | | comment | Adds a `$comment` to the query that shows in the [profiler](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/database-profiler.md#std-label-profiler) logs. | | explain | Adds explain output based on the verbosity mode provided. | | hint | Forces the query optimizer to use specific indexes in the query. | | limit | Sets a limit of documents returned in the result set. | | max | The exclusive upper bound for a specific index. | | maxAwaitTimeMS | The maximum amount of time for the server to wait on new documents to satisfy a tailable cursor query. Requires `tailable` and `awaitData` to be `true`. | | maxTimeMS | The maximum amount of time (in milliseconds) the server should allow the query to run. | | min | The inclusive lower bound for a specific index. | | noCursorTimeout | Whether the server should timeout the cursor after a period of inactivity (by default 10 minutes). | | projection | Specifies the fields to return in the documents that match the query filter. You can specify projection in two ways for [`find()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/db.collection.find.md#mongodb-method-db.collection.find) and [`findOne()`:](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/db.collection.findone.md#mongodb-method-db.collection.findOne) Setting the `projection` parameter; Setting the `options` parameter to `projection` If you specify both parameters, the `projection` parameter takes precedence. To use `options.projection`, set the `projection` parameter to `null` or `undefined`. | | readConcern | Specifies the read concern level for the query. | | readPreference | Specifies the read preference level for the query. | | returnKey | Whether only the index keys are returned for a query. | | showRecordId | If the `$recordId` field is added to the returned documents. The `$recordId` indicates the position of the document in the result set. | | skip | How many documents to skip before returning the first document in the result set. | | sort | The order of the documents returned in the result set. Fields specified in the sort, must have an index. | | tailable | Indicates if the cursor is tailable. Tailable cursors remain open after the intial results of the query are exhausted. Tailable cursors are only available on [Capped Collections.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/capped-collections.md#std-label-manual-capped-collection) | — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/db.collection.find.md#options · keywords: index, index key, query planner, cursor.allowDiskUse(), tailable, true
- [passage] Given these queries, the index with the [partial filter expression](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-partial.md#std-label-partial-index-query-coverage) can support query operation 2 but *not* support query operation 1. Since the indexes available to support query operation 1 differs from query operation 2, the two queries have different `planCacheKey`. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/query-plans.md#plancachekey · keywords: index, partial index, planCacheKey
- [passage] You can have a clustered index and add [secondary indexes](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/glossary.md#std-term-secondary-index) to a clustered collection. Clustered indexes differ from secondary indexes: — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/clustered-collections.md#behavior · keywords: mongodb-compound-index-design
- [passage] Storing the collection's documents in index order can provide benefits for storage and performance compared to traditional collections and their related regular indexes. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/clustered-collections.md · keywords: mongodb-compound-index-design
- [passage] Indexes improve read performance, but a large number of indexes can negatively impact write performance since indexes must be updated during writes. If your collection already has several indexes, consider this tradeoff of read and write performance when deciding whether to create new indexes. Examine whether a query for such a collection can be modified to take advantage of existing indexes, as well as whether a query occurs often enough to justify the cost of a new index. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/performance-advisor.md#index-considerations · keywords: mongodb-compound-index-design
- [passage] The argument to [`$elemMatch`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/projection/elemmatch.md#mongodb-projection-proj.-elemMatch) matches elements of the array that `$elemMatch` is projecting. If you specify an equality with a field name to `$elemMatch`, it attempts to match objects within the array. For example, `$elemMatch` attempts to match objects, instead of scalar values, within the array for the following in the projection: — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/projection/elemMatch.md#elemmatch-https-www-mongodb-com-docs-manual-reference-operator-projection-elemmatch-md-mongodb-projection-proj-elemmatch-with-multiple-fields · keywords: $elemMatch

## Facts and statements

- [passage] If you have a collection that has both a compound index and an index on its prefix (for example, `{ a: 1, b: 1 }` and `{ a: 1 }`), if neither index has a [sparse](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-sparse.md#std-label-index-type-sparse) or [unique](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-unique.md#std-label-index-type-unique) constraint, you can remove the index on the prefix (`{ a: 1 }`). MongoDB uses the compound index in all of the situations that it would have used the prefix index. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-compound.md#index-prefixes · keywords: compound index, index, index prefix, sparse index, { a: 1, b: 1 }, { a: 1 }
- [fact] MongoDB's current manual presents ESR as a guideline with an explicit exception. If the range predicate is very selective, putting it before the sort fields (ERS) reduces the number of documents sorted, and the query accepts an in-memory sort. If avoiding in-memory sorts is critical, use ESR. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/equality-sort-range-rule/ · keywords: ESR rule, compound index, index, sort direction, Compound Indexes and ESR Rule
- [statement] Community report (Jan 2022, no replies captured): on a ~1.2M-document collection, a sparse compound index {A,B,C} serving { A:{$exists:true}, B:false, C:{$lt:date} } logged about 575,000 keys examined and almost 300,000 documents examined. The same keys as a partial index with filter {A:{$exists:true}} gave much better targeting. This is consistent with, but not proof of, the sparse compound rule that documents lacking A are still indexed. — https://www.mongodb.com/community/forums/t/sparse-vs-partial-index-for-compound-index/143869 · keywords: compound index, index, partial index, sparse index, Sparse Indexes
- [passage] For example, consider a compound index `{ temperature: 1, humidity: 1 }` with the following bounds: — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-multikey/multikey-index-bounds.md#compound-bounds-for-a-multikey-index · keywords: $elemMatch, compound index, index, multikey index, { temperature: 1, humidity: 1 }
- [fact] Index intersection does not help a sort that needs an index separate from the query predicate; indexed sorts require a compound index whose key order matches the filter and sort. — https://web.archive.org/web/2024/https://www.mongodb.com/docs/v6.0/core/index-intersection/ · keywords: compound index, index, index anti-pattern, index intersection, Index Intersection
- [passage] For a compound index that includes a 2d index key along with keys of other types, only the 2d index field determines whether the index references a document. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/geospatial/2d.md#sparse-property · keywords: compound index, index, index key, sparse index
- [fact] The ESR guideline orders compound index keys as Equality, then Sort, then Range. Equality fields always come first, and any number of equality keys may appear in any order among themselves. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/equality-sort-range-rule/ · keywords: ESR rule, compound index, index, index key, Compound Indexes and ESR Rule
- [statement] The ESR documentation says equality fields come first and a more selective equality makes the index more efficient. If the range predicate is very selective, place it before the sort fields (ERS), accepting a possible in-memory sort. $in arrays under 201 elements act like equality; 201 or more act like range. — https://mongodb.com/docs/v7.0/tutorial/equality-sort-range-rule · keywords: ESR rule, index, index selectivity, sort direction, Index Selectivity and Covering Queries
- [passage] Compound indexes support sort operations that match either the sort order of the index, or the reverse sort order of the index. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-compound/sort-order.md · keywords: compound index, index, index selectivity, sort direction
- [fact] $elemMatch on the wrong path defeats compounding. For index {ratings.scores.q1: 1, ratings.scores.q2: 1}, ratings: {$elemMatch: {'scores.q1': 2, 'scores.q2': 8}} leaves ratings.scores.q2 unconstrained. Use {'ratings.scores': {$elemMatch: {q1: 2, q2: 8}}} instead. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-multikey/multikey-index-bounds.md · keywords: $elemMatch, index, index anti-pattern, multikey index, Multikey Indexes and Array Query Bounds
- [passage] - Partial indexes include or exclude documents based on the filter expression. The expression can include fields other than index keys, and can specify conditions other than a field existing. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-partial.md#comparison-with-sparse-indexes · keywords: index, index key, partial index, sparse index
- [passage] However, a partial index can also filter on fields other than the index key. For example, a partial index on the `name` field can check for the existence of the `email` field: — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-partial.md#comparison-with-sparse-indexes · keywords: index, index key, partial index, sparse index, name, email
- [fact] The filter may reference fields not in the index keys. Index {name:1} with filter {email:{$exists:true}} serves only queries that also constrain name and require non-null email; {name:1} with {name:{$exists:true}} behaves like a sparse index. — https://mongodb.com/docs/v7.3/core/index-partial · keywords: index, index key, partial index, sparse index, Partial Indexes
- [passage] In a [compound](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-compound.md#std-label-index-type-compound) multikey index, each indexed document can have *at most* one indexed field whose value is an array. Specifically: — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-multikey.md#compound-multikey-indexes · keywords: compound index, index, index key, multikey index · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-multikey/
- [passage] For a query to use a compound index for a sort, the specified sort direction for all keys in the cursor.sort() document must match the index key pattern or match the inverse of the index key pattern. For example, an index key pattern { a: 1, b: -1 } can support a sort on { a: 1, b: -1 } and { a: -1, b: 1 } but not on { a: -1, b: -1 } or {a: 1, b: 1}. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/sort-results-with-indexes/ · keywords: compound index, index, index key, sort direction · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/sort-results-with-indexes.md
- [passage] - Sparse indexes include or exclude documents *solely* based on the presence of the indexed field (or multiple fields, for sparse compound indexes). — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-partial.md#comparison-with-sparse-indexes · keywords: compound index, index, index key, sparse index
- [passage] In most cases, applying the ESR (Equality, Sort, Range) Guideline to arrange the index keys creates a more efficient compound index. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/equality-sort-range-rule/ · keywords: ESR rule, compound index, index, index key · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/equality-sort-range-guideline/
- [passage] In most cases, applying the ESR (Equality, Sort, Range) Guideline to arrange the index keys creates a more efficient [compound index.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-compound.md#std-label-index-type-compound) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/equality-sort-range-guideline.md · keywords: ESR rule, compound index, index, index key · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-compound.md
- [passage] MongoDB compounds the bounds for the `item` key with either the bounds for `"ratings.score"` or the bounds for `"ratings.by"`, depending upon the query predicates and the index key values. MongoDB does not guarantee which bounds it compounds with the `item` field. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-multikey/multikey-index-bounds.md#example-compound-bounds-of-non-array-field-and-multiple-array-fields · keywords: $elemMatch, index, index key, multikey index, item, "ratings.score"
- [passage] - The index keys must share the same field path up to but excluding the field names. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-multikey/multikey-index-bounds.md#compound-bounds-of-multiple-fields-from-the-same-array · keywords: $elemMatch, index, index key, multikey index
- [passage] For a field in an embedded document, the [dotted field name](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/document.md#std-label-document-dot-notation), such as `"a.b.c.d"`, is the field path for `d`. To compound the bounds for index keys from the same array, the `$elemMatch` must be on the path up to *but excluding* the field name itself (meaning `"a.b.c"`). — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-multikey/multikey-index-bounds.md#compound-bounds-of-multiple-fields-from-the-same-array · keywords: $elemMatch, index, index key, multikey index, "a.b.c.d", "a.b.c"
- [passage] The following example shows how MongoDB combines bounds for index keys from the same array. This example uses the `survey2` collection used in the [previous example.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-multikey/multikey-index-bounds.md#std-label-index-bounds-example-non-array-multiple-array) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-multikey/multikey-index-bounds.md#example · keywords: $elemMatch, index, index key, multikey index, survey2
- [fact] Without $elemMatch, {grades: {$gte: 90, $lte: 99}} can be satisfied by different elements, so MongoDB uses only one of [[90, Infinity]] or [[-Infinity, 99]]. The docs say MongoDB gives no guarantee which one. The planner applies the other predicate as a FETCH filter. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-multikey/multikey-index-bounds.md · keywords: $elemMatch, index, multikey index, query planner, Multikey Indexes and Array Query Bounds
- [fact] Index keys from the same array compound their bounds only if (a) the keys share the same path up to but excluding the field names, and (b) the query uses $elemMatch on that path. If the query predicates cover several array fields without $elemMatch, MongoDB compounds the leading scalar field with only one of them and does not guarantee which. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-multikey/multikey-index-bounds.md · keywords: $elemMatch, index, index key, multikey index, Multikey Indexes and Array Query Bounds
- [statement] Safer workaround for complex filters: set a boolean/flag field on write and use a simple equality partialFilterExpression; confirm with explain('executionStats') and hint(). — https://www.mongodb.com/community/forums/t/partial-index-not-covering-or-query-filter/220425 · keywords: index, index anti-pattern, partial index, query planner, Partial Indexes
- [passage] For example, the following operation creates a compound index that indexes only the documents where the `genre` field is `Drama`: — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-partial.md#create-a-partial-index · keywords: compound index, index, partial index, genre, Drama
- [passage] For example, create a compound index on the `data` collection: — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/sort-results-with-indexes.md#sort-and-index-prefix · keywords: compound index, index, index prefix, data · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/sort-results-with-indexes/
- [fact] Example from the MongoDB manual: for find({directors:'David Lynch', runtime:{$lt:130}}).sort({year:1}), the recommended index is {directors:1, year:1, runtime:1}. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/equality-sort-range-rule/ · keywords: ESR rule, compound index, index, Compound Indexes and ESR Rule
- [passage] Given an indexed array field, consider a query that specifies multiple query predicates on the array and uses a [multikey index](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-multikey.md#std-label-index-type-multikey) to fulfill the query. MongoDB can intersect the multikey index bounds if an [`$elemMatch`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/query/elemmatch.md#mongodb-query-op.-elemMatch) operator joins the query predicates. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-multikey/multikey-index-bounds.md#bounds-intersection-for-a-multikey-index · keywords: $elemMatch, index, multikey index, query planner
- [passage] For example, the following operation creates a compound multikey index on the `movies` collection on the `genres` and `title` fields: — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-multikey.md#covered-queries · keywords: covered query, index, multikey index, movies, genres, title · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-multikey/, https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-multikey/create-multikey-index-basic.md
- [passage] For the query optimizer to choose this partial index, the query predicate must include a condition on the `name` field as well as a *non-null* match on the `email` field. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-partial.md#comparison-with-sparse-indexes · keywords: index, partial index, sparse index, name, email
- [fact] MongoDB can combine the scans of two indexes (nested intersections are possible) to answer a query, using either whole indexes or index prefixes. The manual's example combines separate { qty: 1 } and { item: 1 } indexes on an orders collection. — https://web.archive.org/web/2024/https://www.mongodb.com/docs/v6.0/core/index-intersection/ · keywords: index, index intersection, index prefix, Index Intersection
- [statement] Sorting on a multikey-indexed array field adds an in-memory sort stage unless the bounds for all sort fields are [MinKey, MaxKey] and no multikey field bound shares the sort pattern's path prefix. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-multikey.md · keywords: index, multikey index, sort direction, Multikey Indexes and Array Query Bounds
- [fact] Common patterns: index only active/pending status subsets, soft-delete (deletedAt:null), high-value items, conditional uniqueness, and TTL limited to a subset; benefit is smaller index and less write cost for non-matching documents. — https://mongodb.com/docs/v7.3/core/index-partial · keywords: covered query, index, partial index, Partial Indexes
- [passage] - To learn how to create efficient compound indexes, see [The ESR (Equality, Sort, Range) Guideline.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/equality-sort-range-guideline.md#std-label-esr-indexing-guideline) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-compound/create-compound-index.md#learn-more · keywords: ESR rule, compound index, index
- [fact] Official guidance: schema designs should not rely on index intersection; compound indexes should be used instead. Independent writers agree (a well-designed compound index almost always beats intersection; 'if you think you need index intersection, you probably need better compound indexes'). — https://web.archive.org/web/2024/https://www.mongodb.com/docs/v6.0/core/index-intersection/ · keywords: compound index, index, index intersection, Index Intersection
- [passage] The following example shows how MongoDB uses bounds intersection to define a smaller range of values to query, resulting in improved query performance. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-multikey/multikey-index-bounds.md#example-bounds-intersection · keywords: $elemMatch, index, multikey index

- [passage] **Tip: Remove Redundant Indexes** — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-compound.md#index-prefixes · keywords: index, index anti-pattern, index prefix
- [statement] Cardinality ordering of equality fields is contested. A third-party blog says to place high-cardinality fields first and labels { customerId: 1, status: 1 } good. The MongoDB ESR page says equality fields may appear in any order among themselves and does not mention cardinality. — https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2025-12-15-mongodb-compound-indexes/view · keywords: ESR rule, index, index selectivity, Index Selectivity and Covering Queries
- [statement] Large or unbounded arrays make multikey indexes costly: one entry per element, and index build and read performance degrade as arrays grow. Specific write-amplification claims come from a single third-party blog and are unverified. — https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-03-31-mongodb-how-to-avoid-the-unbounded-array-growth-anti-pattern-in-mong/markdown · keywords: index, index anti-pattern, multikey index, Multikey Indexes and Array Query Bounds
- [fact] Documented partialFilterExpression operators: equality, $exists:true (not false), $gt/$gte/$lt/$lte, $type, $and, $or, $in, $geoWithin, $geoIntersects. Originally (3.1.1) only $exists:true, comparisons, $eq, $type and top-level $and; richer expressions ($elemMatch, $exists:false, $ne/$not) remain an open backlog ticket. — https://mongodb.com/docs/v7.3/core/index-partial · keywords: $elemMatch, index, partial index, Partial Indexes
- [fact] If a sparse index would return an incomplete result set for a query or sort, the planner does not select it unless hint() names it. Example: find().sort({plot:-1}) on a collection where some documents lack plot ignores a sparse index on plot. With hint({plot:1}) the query returns only documents that have plot. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-sparse.md · keywords: index, index anti-pattern, sparse index, Sparse Indexes
- [fact] Hinting a sparse index on a count of all documents (empty predicate) uses the sparse index even though the count is wrong: countDocuments({}, {hint:{rated:1}}) returns only documents that have rated. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-sparse.md · keywords: index, index anti-pattern, sparse index, Sparse Indexes
- [passage] Scans that skip duplicate index keys, counted separately based on whether the scan fetches documents. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/queryStats/ · keywords: index, index anti-pattern, index key, query planner

- [passage] A unique index ensures that the indexed fields do not store duplicate values, and that a value appears at most once for a given field. - [statement] Why the planner avoids intersection (per Franck Pachot's analysis of server source tag r8.2.2): plans that finish their trial first get an 'EOF bonus', intersection plans take a small score penalty, and the productivity metric counts units of work without weighing their cost. Without the penalty the planner would still not pick AND_SORTED. — https://dev.to/franckpachot/mongodb-index-intersection-and-postgresql-bitmap-scan-40a6 · keywords: index, index intersection, Index Intersection

- [statement] Zero read ops does not prove an index is droppable: a unique index can enforce integrity with no reads, and dropping it permits duplicate keys. - [fact] Hide before dropping: db.collection.hideIndex() makes the planner ignore an index; unhideIndex() restores it instantly, avoiding a rebuild. MongoDB's manual workflow is identify, hide, measure, then dropIndexes() if the impact is negative. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/upcoming/core/index-hidden/ · keywords: index, index anti-pattern, Index Anti-Patterns
- [statement] Dropping an index takes a lock that can block operations (Pythian: write lock on the database; Netdata: exclusive collection lock), so schedule drops in low-traffic windows and keep a backup or the index definition to rebuild. — https://www.pythian.com/blog/how-to-find-unused-index-and-drop-them-safely-in-mongodb · keywords: index, index anti-pattern, Index Anti-Patterns
- [fact] Query selectivity is how well a predicate filters out documents. An equality match on unique _id is highly selective. $ne and $nin match much of the index, so with an index they may perform no better than a collection scan. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/query-optimization/ · keywords: index, index selectivity, Index Selectivity and Covering Queries

- [passage] The index stores the value of a specific field or set of fields, ordered by the value of the field. - [passage] Partial indexes only index the documents in a collection that meet a specified filter expression. - [passage] "Sort" determines the order for results. - [passage] If $in has fewer than 201 array elements, the elements are expanded and then merged in the sort order specified for the index using a SORT_MERGE stage. This improves performance for small arrays. In this case, $in is similar to an equality predicate with ESR. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/equality-sort-range-rule/ · keywords: ESR rule, index · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/equality-sort-range-guideline/, https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/equality-sort-range-guideline.md
- [passage] If $in has 201 elements or more, the elements are ordered like a range operator. In this case, the performance improvement for small arrays isn't realized. It isn't possible for the subsequent fields in the index to be used for sorting, and $in is similar to a range predicate with ESR. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/equality-sort-range-rule/ · keywords: ESR rule, index · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/equality-sort-range-guideline/, https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/equality-sort-range-guideline.md

- [passage] 2d indexes are always [sparse](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-sparse.md#std-label-index-type-sparse) and ignore the [sparse](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-sparse.md#std-label-index-type-sparse) option. - [passage] An aggregation pipeline can use [indexes](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/indexes.md#std-label-indexes) from the input collection to improve performance. Using an index limits the amount of documents a stage processes. Ideally, an index can [cover](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/query-optimization.md#std-label-read-operations-covered-query) the stage query. A covered query has especially high performance, since the index returns all matching documents. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/aggregation-pipeline-optimization.md#indexes · keywords: covered query, index
- [passage] - An index on the grouping field that matches the `$sort` order returns all of the field values needed for the `$group` stage, making it a covered query. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/aggregation-pipeline-optimization.md#indexes · keywords: covered query, index, $sort, $group

- [passage] | Projection | Description | | --- | --- | | `<field>: <1 or true>` | Specifies the inclusion of a field. If you specify a non-zero integer for the projection value, the operation treats the value as `true`. | | `<field>: <0 or false>` | Specifies the exclusion of a field. | | `"<field>.$": <1 or true>` | Uses the [`$`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/projection/positional.md#mongodb-projection-proj.-) array projection operator to return the first element that matches the query condition on the array field. If you specify a non-zero integer for the projection value, the operation treats the value as `true`. Not available for [views.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/views.md#std-label-views-landing-page) | | `<field>: <array projection>` | Uses the array projection operators ([`$elemMatch`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/projection/elemmatch.md#mongodb-projection-proj.-elemMatch), [`$slice`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/projection/slice.md#mongodb-projection-proj.-slice)) to specify the array elements to include. Not available for [views.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/views.md#std-label-views-landing-page) | | `<field>: <aggregation expression>` | Specifies the value of the projected field. With the use of [aggregation expressions and syntax](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/mql/expressions.md#std-label-aggregation-expressions), including the use of literals and aggregation variables, you can project new fields or project existing fields with new values. If you specify a non-numeric, non-boolean literal (such as a literal string or an array or an operator expression) for the projection value, the field is projected with the new value, for example:`{ field: [ 1, 2, 3, "$someExistingField" ] }`; `{ field: "New String Value" }`; `{ field: { status: "Active", total: { $sum: "$existingArray" } } }`; To project a literal value for a field, use the [`$literal`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/literal.md#mongodb-expression-exp.-literal) aggregation expression, for example:`{ field: { $literal: 5 } }`; `{ field: { $literal: true } }`; `{ field: { $literal: { fieldWithValue0: 0, fieldWithValue1: 1 } } }` | — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/db.collection.findOneAndUpdate.md#projection · keywords: $elemMatch, <field>: <1 or true>, true, <field>: <0 or false>, "<field>.$": <1 or true>, <field>: <array projection> · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/db.collection.findOneAndDelete.md, https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/db.collection.findAndModify.md, https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/db.collection.findOneAndReplace.md, https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/db.collection.find.md

- [passage] - The field you choose for your hashed shard key should have a high [cardinality](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/sharding-choose-a-shard-key.md#std-label-shard-key-range), meaning a large number of different values. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/index-hashed/create.md#choose-a-hashed-shard-key · keywords: index selectivity
- [passage] Depending on the distribution of data in the cluster and the selectivity of the query, [`mongos`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/program/mongos.md#mongodb-binary-bin.mongos) may still perform a [broadcast operation](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/sharded-cluster-query-router.md#std-label-sharding-mongos-broadcast) to fulfill these queries. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/sharded-cluster-query-router.md#targeted-operations · keywords: index selectivity, mongos
- [passage] The following query filter uses the [`$elemMatch`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/query/elemMatch.md#mongodb-query-op.-elemMatch) operator to find all documents where at least one value in the `scores` array is greater than `80` and less than `90`: — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-ui/query/filter.md#match-by-array-conditions · keywords: $elemMatch, scores, 80, 90 · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/compass/query/filter.md
